academic_source: Fama & French (1987, Journal of Business) and Erb & Harvey (2006, Financial Analysts Journal) - commodity futures term-structure/backwardation risk premium
specification: sign(ln(front_close/next_close)); backwardation (front>next) -> LONG, contango (front<next) -> SHORT; stop-and-reverse, next-bar execution; only front contract traded
sample_period: 2025-11-25 to 2026-09-11 (199 calendar bars, 197 days with a valid front/next signal)

buy_and_hold_benchmark.description: Simple long-only buy-and-hold of the same front contract over the same window (entry at bar[1].open, exit at bar[-1].close, same base-scenario cost model, single round trip) -- computed to check whether the roll-yield SIGNAL adds anything beyond simply being long a market that happened to be in backwardation almost the entire time.

conclusion: NOT a demonstrated edge. The strategy is net positive and strikingly cost-robust (net barely moves from base to stress scenario, $4108->$4084, because holding periods are long so transaction costs are a tiny fraction of P&L -- a genuine structural property of carry-style strategies). But n=6 trades is far too few to mean anything statistically (naive t-stat ~0.96, itself not HAC-adjusted and not meaningful at this sample size), AND the strategy's net P&L is 98.6% of a naive buy-and-hold benchmark over the identical window. WTI was in backwardation 186 of 197 days (94%) while also rallying hard (58.36 -> 100.04, +71%) -- the roll-yield signal was net long almost the whole period simply because backwardation was persistent, so this result cannot be distinguished from the strategy having accidentally just captured market beta. A genuine test of the term-structure risk premium needs either (a) many more independent regime changes (multi-year data, per section 14) so LONG and SHORT periods are both well-sampled, or (b) a cross-sectional design (ranking multiple commodities by basis and going long the most-backwardated / short the most-contango, as Erb & Harvey 2006 actually do) rather than a single-instrument time-series version, which this project's single-instrument-at-a-time architecture does not yet support.
